prompt: Why are amides so abundant in living organisms?

choices.text: They are stable in the aqueous conditions found in living organisms
They are the most reactive carboxylic acid derivatives
choices.why: Amides are the least reactive of the common acid derivatives.

choices.text: Cells make them from acid chlorides and amines
choices.why: Acid chlorides react too rapidly with water to exist in living organisms.

choices.text: They react quickly with water, releasing energy
choices.why: The opposite is true: amides are stable in water, and their hydrolysis needs harsh conditions or an enzyme.

explanation: Proteins, nucleic acids, and many drugs contain amide groups. Amides are abundant because they are stable in aqueous conditions; they are the least reactive of the common acid derivatives.

prompt: Which amines react with acid chlorides to give amides?

choices.text: Ammonia, monosubstituted amines, and disubstituted amines

choices.why: Monosubstituted and disubstituted amines react too, giving N-substituted amides.
Trisubstituted amines are the ones that can't be used.

choices.text: Ammonia and all amines, including trisubstituted amines
choices.why: Trisubstituted amines (R3N) can't be used (Section 21.4).

explanation: Amides are usually prepared by reaction of an amine with an acid chloride. Ammonia, monosubstituted amines, and disubstituted amines all undergo the reaction.

prompt: How do the conditions for amide hydrolysis compare with those for hydrolysis of acid chlorides or esters?

choices.text: More extreme conditions: heating in aqueous acid or base
Milder conditions: amides hydrolyze faster, even in cold water
choices.why: Amides are the least reactive acid derivatives. Their hydrolysis requires heating in aqueous acid or base.

choices.text: Amides can be hydrolyzed only in acid, never in base
choices.why: Amides are hydrolyzed by heating in either aqueous acid or aqueous base, although base is more difficult.

choices.text: Amides can't be hydrolyzed at all, even by enzymes
choices.why: Amides are hydrolyzed on heating with acid or base, and protease enzymes hydrolyze the amide links of proteins.

explanation: Amides are hydrolyzed to carboxylic acids plus ammonia or an amine on heating in aqueous acid or aqueous base. The conditions are more extreme than those for hydrolysis of acid chlorides or esters, but the mechanisms are similar.

prompt: Which carboxylic acid and amine does hydrolysis of N-methylacetamide, CH3CONHCH3, give?

choices.why: Hydrolysis breaks the bond between the carbonyl carbon and nitrogen, not the N–CH3 bond.
The nitrogen keeps its methyl group, so the amine released is methylamine.
The acyl group, CH3CO–, has two carbons and becomes acetic acid.

explanation: Amide hydrolysis gives a carboxylic acid plus ammonia or an amine. The C–N bond to the carbonyl carbon breaks, so CH3CONHCH3 gives acetic acid and methylamine. Depending on the conditions, the products may end up as the ammonium ion or the carboxylate ion.

prompt: In the acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of an amide, why is a proton transferred from oxygen to nitrogen after water adds?

choices.text: To make the nitrogen a better leaving group
To make the oxygen a better nucleophile
choices.why: Water has already added by that point. The proton transfer prepares the nitrogen to leave.

choices.text: To form an iminium ion that is then reduced
choices.why: Iminium ions form in the LiAlH4 reduction of amides, not in hydrolysis.

choices.text: To deprotonate the carboxylic acid product
choices.why: Deprotonation of the carboxylic acid drives basic hydrolysis. In acid, a proton is moved onto nitrogen.

explanation: Acidic hydrolysis occurs by nucleophilic addition of water to the protonated amide, followed by transfer of a proton from oxygen to nitrogen to make the nitrogen a better leaving group, and then elimination.

prompt: In acidic amide hydrolysis, what shifts the equilibrium toward the products?

choices.text: Protonation of the NH3 released in the final step
Deprotonation of the carboxylic acid by ammonia
choices.why: That is the driving force in basic hydrolysis.
Amide ion is a very poor leaving group. In acid the nitrogen leaves as NH3 after being protonated.

choices.text: Reduction of the carboxylic acid by the acid catalyst
choices.why: Nothing is reduced in a hydrolysis. The equilibrium is shifted by protonating the NH3.

explanation: The steps of acidic amide hydrolysis are reversible, with the equilibrium shifted toward product by protonation of NH3 in the final step.

prompt: Why is basic hydrolysis of an amide substantially more difficult than acid-catalyzed hydrolysis?

choices.text: Amide ion, ^−NH2, is a very poor leaving group
Hydroxide ion can't add to an amide carbonyl group
choices.why: Basic hydrolysis starts with nucleophilic addition of OH− to the amide carbonyl group.

choices.text: The carboxylic acid product can't be deprotonated in base
choices.why: It is deprotonated, and that final deprotonation drives the reaction.

choices.text: Ammonia protonates the hydroxide ion and stops the reaction
choices.why: Ammonia acts as a base in the last step, deprotonating the carboxylic acid.

explanation: Basic hydrolysis occurs by addition of OH− to the amide carbonyl, elimination of amide ion (^−NH2), and deprotonation of the carboxylic acid by ammonia. Because amide ion is a very poor leaving group, the elimination step is difficult.

prompt: In basic amide hydrolysis, what shifts the equilibrium toward the products?

choices.text: Deprotonation of the carboxylic acid formed
Protonation of ammonia to ammonium ion
choices.why: That is the driving force in acidic hydrolysis.
Iminium ions form in LiAlH4 reductions of amides, not in hydrolysis.

choices.text: Loss of water from the tetrahedral intermediate
choices.why: In hydrolysis water or hydroxide adds; the leaving group is amide ion, and the final step is deprotonation of the acid.

explanation: The steps of basic amide hydrolysis are reversible, with the equilibrium shifted toward product by the final deprotonation of the carboxylic acid.

prompt: How do protease enzymes hydrolyze the amide linkages of dietary proteins?

choices.text: An enzyme –OH forms an acyl enzyme intermediate, which is then hydrolyzed
Hydride from the enzyme reduces each amide link to an amine group
choices.why: Proteases hydrolyze amides; they don't reduce them. Amide reduction to amines uses LiAlH4 in the laboratory.

choices.text: The enzyme first converts each amide link into a reactive acid chloride
choices.why: Acid chlorides can't exist in living organisms. The enzyme forms an acyl enzyme intermediate instead.

choices.text: Water adds directly to each amide, with no intermediate involving the enzyme
choices.why: The section says an alcohol group of the enzyme reacts first, giving an acyl enzyme intermediate.

explanation: Protein digestion begins with amide hydrolysis catalyzed by proteases, by a mechanism almost identical to fat hydrolysis. An alcohol group in the enzyme carries out a nucleophilic acyl substitution on the amide link to give an acyl enzyme intermediate, which is then hydrolyzed.

prompt: N-Methyldodecanamide, CH3(CH2)10CONHCH3, is treated with LiAlH4 and then water. What is the product?

choices.why: Other acid derivatives are reduced to alcohols, but amides give amines. The C=O becomes CH2 and the nitrogen stays.
The C–N bond isn't broken. The carbonyl group is reduced all the way to CH2.
That would be the hydrolysis product. LiAlH4 reduces the amide.

explanation: Amides are reduced by LiAlH4 to amines rather than alcohols. The net effect is conversion of the amide C=O into a CH2 group, so N-methyldodecanamide gives dodecylmethylamine (95%).

prompt: What intermediate forms during the LiAlH4 reduction of an amide?

choices.why: Aldehydes are intermediates in the reduction of esters and acid chlorides. In an amide reduction the oxygen is expelled instead of the nitrogen.
Acyl chlorosulfites form when carboxylic acids react with SOCl2.
Acyl enzyme intermediates form during enzyme-catalyzed hydrolysis of amides and esters.

explanation: Hydride adds to the amide carbonyl group, and the oxygen is expelled as an aluminate anion leaving group to give an iminium ion. The iminium ion is then reduced by LiAlH4 to the amine.

prompt: What does LiAlH4 reduction of a lactam (a cyclic amide) give?

choices.why: A lactone is a cyclic ester. Reduction doesn't replace the ring nitrogen with oxygen.

choices.text: An amino alcohol formed by opening the ring
choices.why: The C=O is converted into a CH2 group and the ring stays intact.
The carbonyl group is reduced to CH2, and the nitrogen stays in the ring.

explanation: Amide reduction works with both acyclic and cyclic amides (lactams). The ring C=O becomes CH2, so it is a good method for preparing cyclic amines.

prompt: Which amide would you reduce with LiAlH4 to prepare N-ethylaniline, C6H5NHCH2CH3?

choices.why: Reducing benzamide gives C6H5CH2NH2, with a CH2 between the ring and nitrogen.
Reducing this amide gives C6H5CH2NHCH2CH3, which has an extra CH2 between the ring and nitrogen.
Reducing this amide gives C6H5NHCH3, with a methyl group instead of an ethyl group on nitrogen.

explanation: To find the amide, look for a CH2 next to the nitrogen and replace it with C=O. In N-ethylaniline, the ethyl CH2 next to nitrogen becomes C=O, giving N-phenylacetamide (Worked Example 21.7.1).

prompt: Bromocyclohexane is converted into (N,N-dimethylaminomethyl)cyclohexane, C6H11CH2N(CH3)2, with LiAlH4 reduction of an amide as the key step. Which amide is reduced?

choices.why: Reducing this amide gives C6H11CH2CH2N(CH3)2, which has one carbon too many between the ring and nitrogen.
Reducing this amide gives C6H11CH2NH2, with no methyl groups on nitrogen.
Reducing this amide gives C6H11NHCH2CH3, with the nitrogen bonded directly to the ring.

explanation: Replace the CH2 next to nitrogen with C=O: C6H11CH2N(CH3)2 comes from C6H11CON(CH3)2. The full route is 1. Mg; 2. CO2, then H3O+; 3. SOCl2; 4. (CH3)2NH; 5. LiAlH4 (Exercise 21.7.2).

prompt: What amine forms when N,N-diethylacetamide, CH3CON(CH2CH3)2, is reduced with LiAlH4 and then treated with water?

choices.why: Amide reduction doesn't break the C–N bond. The C=O becomes CH2 and the nitrogen keeps all three groups.
Both carbons of the acetyl group stay. The C=O becomes CH2, so CH3CO– becomes an ethyl group, CH3CH2–.
The oxygen doesn't stay. It is expelled as an aluminate leaving group, and the carbon ends up as CH2, not CH–OH.

explanation: LiAlH4 converts the amide carbonyl group into a methylene group (C=O → CH2). The acetyl group becomes an ethyl group, so N,N-diethylacetamide gives triethylamine.
